title: The Variable Vault — Giving Names to Magic!

learningObjectives.description: Explain that a variable is a name referring to a value.
Assign a value to a name using =.
Store a string and an integer.
Display a variable’s value with print().
Change the value associated with a name.
Recognize simple valid names and use readable snake_case.

conceptExplanations: A variable is a name referring to a value. The labeled-box picture is a learning aid: Python names refer to objects; they are not physical boxes.
Use = for assignment: familiar = "Hexi" associates a string with a name. potions = 3 associates an integer. Assignment itself produces no printed output.
print(familiar) displays the stored value; print("familiar") displays the literal name. Names must be assigned before use and are case-sensitive.
Reassignment makes the same name refer to a new value. Earlier output does not change. Print before and after the assignment to observe both values.

Python names can start with a letter or underscore, followed by letters, digits, or underscores. No spaces, hyphens, or reserved keywords. Lowercase snake_case is a convention; uppercase is legal. This activity supports ASCII names up to 40 characters and reserves print to avoid shadowing it.

This is a bounded source-text model, not a Python interpreter. Only literal strings, small integers, assignments, and print(variable) are recognized. Other valid Python forms can be unsupported. No source is executed or transmitted.

examples.explanation: The name familiar refers to the string Hexi. print(familiar) displays its value, not its name.
3 is an integer. "3" would be a string; they look alike when printed but have different types.
Statements are read from top to bottom. Reassignment changes what the same name refers to; it does not print anything by itself.

practiceTasks.instruction: Give a variable the string "Hexi", then print that variable. Use one assignment and one print on separate lines.
Store the integer 3 in a variable, then print that variable. Do not put the number in quotes. Use one assignment and one print.
Store the integer 2 in a variable and print it. Reassign the same name to the integer 5, then print it again. Use two assignments and two prints.

Create two different variables: a string with the value "Moon Tea" and an integer with the value 4. Print the text variable, then the number variable, on separate lines. Use two assignments and two prints.

successCriteria: Use the task’s required value types, assignments, and variable prints.
Match expected output exactly, including one newline per print.
For reassignment, print the same variable before and after changing it.
evaluationCriteria: At most 500 characters and 12 lines; no indented statements.
ASCII identifiers up to 40 characters, plain single/double-quoted strings without escapes, and integers from -9999 to 9999.
Reject all unsupported forms, imports, expressions, calls, and direct-literal prints without executing source.
Passing establishes only task-pattern performance, not mastery, execution, or permanent learning.

errorFeedback.empty: Start with an assignment, then print the variable on a new line.
errorFeedback.unsupported-syntax: This checker accepts only one literal assignment or print(variable) per line: plain quoted strings and integers from -9999 to 9999. No expressions, escapes, comments, or other Python forms are supported.
errorFeedback.output-mismatch: The supported statements are recognized, but their inferred output differs. Check values, case, spaces, and statement order.
errorFeedback.too-long: Keep this small exercise to 500 characters and 12 lines or fewer.
errorFeedback.correct: Your written assignments match the task and expected output under this restricted checker. Python was not executed.
errorFeedback.invalid-name: Use an ASCII letter or underscore first, followed by letters, digits, or underscores (up to 40 characters here). Avoid Python keywords and the name print. Lowercase snake_case is recommended, not required.
errorFeedback.assignment: Use a single = for assignment. == compares values; it does not assign them. This activity does not support :=.
errorFeedback.quotes: Use a plain quoted string, like "Hexi", or an integer, like 3. Copying another variable is valid Python but outside this exercise’s literal-only checker.
errorFeedback.undefined-name: Assign this variable before printing it. Names are case-sensitive: potions and Potions are different names.
errorFeedback.print-variable: Print one assigned variable: print(familiar). A quoted name prints literal text. Expressions, multiple arguments, and direct literals are outside this task.
errorFeedback.indentation: Start these simple statements at the left edge. This lesson does not use indented blocks.
errorFeedback.task-shape: Follow this task’s required assignments and prints. Reassignment needs the same variable twice, with one print before and one after the change; each other task needs its stated value types.

safety.performanceClaim: Passing demonstrates performance under a restricted text checker, not Python execution, mastery, humanlike understanding, or retained agent learning.
